name: Custom PEEK/Medpor jaw implants

lead: Custom jaw implants build a more defined jawline to your own measurements. A surgeon or design team models the implant on a 3D copy of your skull from a CT scan, and it is made in porous polyethylene (Medpor) or the rigid polymer PEEK and placed through the mouth. People use them to add width, height or projection at the jaw angle and ramus, often with chin and cheek implants.

The implant sits on the outside of the bone and adds volume. On forums, members share surgeon lists, post design files and compare planned millimeter dimensions, and custom implants are a common alternative to jaw-moving surgery. Published outcome data for purely cosmetic use is limited.

paras: People typically go through a design stage, planning target proportions with the surgeon before manufacture. The change becomes visible as swelling settles. Forum posters stress careful surgeon selection and design choices.

Risks of any facial implant include infection, displacement, asymmetry and nerve injury, and an implant can need removal. Forum posters note a wider jaw is not always more aesthetic and that some designs produce a rounder rather than more angular jaw.

angle.text: A wider, more defined jawline built to fit your skull. An implant designed from your CT scan adds width or length at the jaw angle and ramus, and the change is visible once swelling settles. Published outcome data for purely cosmetic use is limited.

lead: Custom PEEK and Medpor jaw implants are patient-specific implants designed from a CT scan of the facial skeleton and placed on the bone to add width, vertical height or projection to the jaw angle, ramus and sometimes the chin. People use them to get a stronger, more defined or more angular jawline, often as an alternative to jaw-moving surgery, and often combined with cheek or chin implants. Two materials come up most: porous polyethylene, sold as Medpor, and polyetheretherketone (PEEK), a rigid thermoplastic used in other medical implants such as cranial plates.[1][2]

In looksmaxxing forums, custom implants are discussed as a way to place volume exactly where a particular skull needs it. Members share surgeon names, post 3D design files with millimeter dimensions and ask others to critique the planned shape and chin width.[3][4][5] Some describe a jaw that is widest at the gonial angle and tapers to the chin as the target look; others focus on adding vertical length to a steep jaw angle.[6][7]

Published research on cosmetic jaw-angle implants is small. A 2020 comparison of stock porous polyethylene and custom PEEK implants for mandibular angle contouring in 21 patients reported shorter surgery and better facial symmetry with the custom group, and infections in both groups with no significant difference.[8] Studies of custom PEEK implants in reconstruction and facial feminization surgery report accurate fit and high satisfaction in small series.[9][10]

paras: Unlike off-the-shelf silicone or porous polyethylene jaw implants that come in stock sizes, a custom implant is designed for a single patient from imaging. Forum accounts describe receiving a 3D model from a surgeon showing lateral projection at the jaw angles, added height to the ramus and anterior chin projection, then asking other members for design feedback before surgery.[4]

Variants discussed include angle-only implants, wrap-around designs that connect the jaw angles with the chin, and chin wing designs aimed at vertical and horizontal augmentation.[3][1] Cheek (malar and infraorbital) implants are often planned alongside.[3][6]

PEEK is a semicrystalline thermoplastic with high mechanical and chemical resistance. It was invented in 1978 and brought to market in the early 1980s, and is used in medical implants including partial skull replacements and spinal devices; being radiolucent, it shows clearly on imaging.[2] Medpor is a porous polyethylene that tissue can grow into. Surgeon commentary describing the 2020 comparison notes that stock porous polyethylene implants needed modification during surgery while custom PEEK implants did not.[8]

Forum users describe custom implants as an option for people who want a stronger jawline but do not want or cannot have orthognathic surgery. Threads cover surgeon selection, 3D design, millimeter dimensions and target facial ratios.[3][4] Surgeons named in these threads include several US craniofacial surgeons and some practitioners in Europe, with discussion centered on experience with large custom designs.[3]

Design philosophy is a recurring topic. One poster argued that many jaw implants produce a round, wide jaw and that the ideal is a jaw widest at the gonial angle that tapers to a sharp chin, paired with cheek implants.[6] Another poster with a history of jaw surgery posted a planned design with specified millimeter projections and asked for help judging chin width and squareness.[4] A UK poster wanted added vertical length along the jaw blending into the chin, and another member suggested he might also need jaw-moving surgery.[7]

A 2020 report in the Journal of Craniofacial Surgery compared stock porous polyethylene (12 patients) and CAD/CAM PEEK patient-specific implants (9 patients) for mandibular angle contouring. As summarized by surgeon Barry Eppley, custom implants took about 15 minutes less to place, gave greater facial symmetry, and postoperative infections occurred in both groups without a significant difference.[8]

In reconstruction, a 2020 series of six patients with 10 patient-specific implants (8 PEEK, 2 titanium) at sites including the mandible reported no postoperative complications, satisfaction with function and appearance, and a mean follow-up of 9.4 months; the authors named cost as the main drawback.[9] A 2026 review of 33 transfeminine patients who received custom PEEK malar implants measured about 5.5 mm of added malar projection.[10] These studies cover reconstruction, feminization and cheek implants rather than cosmetic jaw widening specifically.

lore.intro: Custom jaw implants are discussed on looksmax.org mainly as a route to a wider, longer or more angular jaw, with threads about choosing surgeons and critiquing 3D designs.[3][6][4]

claims.claim: A custom implant can give a more refined jaw than stock implants
The jaw should be designed to a target ratio such as bigonial to bizygomatic width
Implants can compensate for a jaw left undefined by previous surgery
Implants alone may not suit every jaw; some need jaw-moving surgery
